findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — [P1, confidence 100] `if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)) {` and `granted.add(groupResource.getId());` confuse authorization resource IDs with group IDs: the schema stores each group ID in the resource name and `hasPermission` looks up that name, so enumerated individual resources are evaluated against the all-groups fallback and any granted authorization resource IDs are passed to user membership searches/counts as nonexistent group IDs, omitting the permitted users.

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real bug in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(). The code at line 121 iterates over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. However, looking at the AdminPermissionsSchema, resources are created with the group's ID as the resource name (via resolveGroup returning group.getId()), but the resource's own ID is a different internal identifier. The method should be collecting the resource names (which are the actual group IDs) rather than the resource IDs. Additionally, when only an all-groups permission exists without individual group permissions, only the sentinel 'Groups' resource type resource would be found, and its ID would be incorrectly added to the set. This would cause the user search to filter by incorrect group IDs, making authorized members disappear from results.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java line 123, when iterating over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, the code calls `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. However, examining AdminPermissionsSchema.java, the resource ID for groups is the group's actual ID (see resolveGroup method which returns group.getId()). But the issue is that resourceStore.findByType returns Resource objects, and groupResource.getId() returns the Resource's internal ID, not the group ID that was used as the resource name. Looking at getOrCreateResource in AdminPermissionsSchema, the resource is created with `id` as the name (line 117: `resource.setName(name)` where name comes from resolveGroup which returns group.getId()). So the resource name contains the group ID, but groupResource.getId() returns the Resource object's ID, not the name. This means the set will contain wrong IDs. The correct call should be groupResource.getName() to get the actual group ID.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java line 70, the canManage() method returns true if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) returns true. This means having either VIEW or MANAGE scope on all-groups grants canManage() = true. In GroupsResource.java, addTopLevelGroup() calls auth.groups().requireManage() which checks canManage(). So a user with only VIEW scope on all-groups would pass the requireManage() check and be able to create top-level groups or modify group hierarchy. This is a security bug - VIEW scope should not grant management capabilities. The canManage() method should only check for MANAGE scope, not VIEW.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a test design issue in testManageGroupMembership(). The test first attempts to join 'no-such' group (which fails with ForbiddenException), then creates both MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP permission for users AND MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission for the group, then successfully joins topGroup. The concern is valid: the test doesn't isolate whether MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP on the group is actually required, since both permissions are granted before the successful operation. A proper test would verify that having only the user permission without the group permission still fails. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for the new permission logic, though it's about test quality rather than a bug in the implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a legitimate test coverage concern. The diff shows RealmAdminPermissionsConfig now grants QUERY_GROUPS role to myadmin (line 36). Looking at GroupPermissions.canList() (line 149), it returns true if user has QUERY_GROUPS role OR canView(). The new GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest tests rely on this config, but because QUERY_GROUPS is always granted, the tests don't verify that listing works with ONLY fine-grained VIEW permission (without the role). This is a valid observation about incomplete test coverage for the new V2 permission path where canList() should work via canView() alone. However, the finding overstates the issue - the tests do verify VIEW permissions work for actual group access, just not specifically for the canList() path without the role.
